study_identification.title: Revealing Individual Neuroanatomical Heterogeneity in Alzheimer Disease Using Neuroanatomical Normative Modeling

study_characteristics.study_objective: The study aimed to use neuroanatomical normative modeling to characterize individual differences in cortical thickness in AD, MCI, and controls. It also assessed relationships between this heterogeneity and cognitive/biological markers, and its potential to predict MCI-to-AD conversion.
study_characteristics.study_design_other: Primarily cross-sectional, with a longitudinal component for the MCI to AD conversion analysis.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Hierarchical Bayesian regression was used to predict cortical thickness per region, adaptively pooling parameter estimates across sites via a shared prior. This approach simultaneously accounts for intersite variation. The reference model parameters were then recalibrated to the ADNI dataset using 70% of healthy controls from each ADNI site.
site_effect_handling_detail.reason: The text provides a detailed description of the HBR method used for handling site effects.
site_effect_handling_detail.supporting_text: A hierarchical Bayesian regression model was trained on multisite data to generate normative models per region using the covariates age and sex. This was based on the population variation in the reference data set (training data), which adaptively pools parameter estimates across sites via a shared prior over regression parameters across sites. 27 This simultaneously accounts for intersite variation and allows sites to borrow strength from one another in a fully Bayesian framework.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Group differences in tOC and Z-scores were tested with linear regression. Dissimilarity was measured with Hamming distance and compared between groups. Associations between tOC and cognitive/CSF markers were tested with linear regression adjusting for covariates. MCI-to-AD conversion risk was assessed using Cox proportional hazards regression.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Individualized normative maps of cortical thickness reveal heterogeneous patterns of atrophy in AD, and the extent of this individual deviation is associated with cognitive decline, AD biomarkers, and risk of conversion from MCI to AD.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Patients with AD had significantly more outlier regions (median 12) than MCI (median 4) or controls (median 2) and were more dissimilar from each other. A greater total outlier count (tOC) was associated with worse memory and executive function, lower CSF Aβ, and higher p-tau. For every 10-point increase in tOC, the risk of MCI-to-AD conversion within 3 years increased by 31.4% (HR 1.028). Notably, even patients matched on clinical and demographic factors showed markedly different spatial patterns of cortical atrophy.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: The reference dataset, while large, may not be fully representative of a healthy population, and ADNI participants may not reflect the general clinical population. The use of multiple FreeSurfer versions could introduce noise. The study is primarily cross-sectional, limiting insights into temporal dynamics of heterogeneity. The analysis was limited to cortical thickness and did not include other metrics like subcortical volumes.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: The study highlights that individualized measures of neuroanatomy (tOC) are sensitive to non-imaging disease markers and progression. The authors propose that these individual neuroanatomical maps could serve as a marker of AD state, potentially indexing disease progression or treatment effectiveness in a personalized manner.

general_notes.general_notes: The study used a transfer learning approach, recalibrating a normative model trained on a large external dataset to the specific sites within the ADNI cohort. This is a key methodological feature for handling multi-site data with small sample sizes per site.
